newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Kuwait Airways says could return to profit.
newsitem.headline: Kuwait Airways says could return to profit.

text.p: Kuwait Airways Corp (KAC) said on Monday it could return to profit if the Kuwaiti government allowed it to raise air fares to match regional rates and helped finance part of huge post-Gulf War reconstruction costs.
"There are measures that can be implemented today so that KAC becomes profitable again," said Ahmad al-Meshari, chairman of the state-owned firm which is earmarked for privatisation.

KAC could "at least" return to the black "if the state changes price levels and helps KAC with some of what was spent on reconstruction," he added. "We are not demanding that the state pays the debt but it is a method to return us to profitability".

In the first half of the 1996/97 fiscal year to December 1996, KAC had total income of 98.5 million dinars ($325.1 million) compared with expenditures of 111 million dinars. Some 9.1 million dinars of the deficit were spent on debt servicing, Meshari said.
KAC made a loss of 35 million dinars in the fiscal year ending June 1996 compared to 27.9 million dinars the previous year.
KAC has presented the government with a three-stage plan to raise fares between 15-25 percent over 18 months -- a move, which if approved, could increase revenue by 17 million dinars, said Meshari.

KAC had not introduced a price rise in a decade while prices for trips originating in Kuwait were 20-50 percent lower than if bought at the other end, he said. In December KAC announced a three percent fare rise to cushion a 40 percent increase in jet fuel prices.
In the first half of 1996/97 KAC paid 2.2 million dinars more than forecast on jet fuel.

KAC, which lost 86 percent of its assets during the 1990-91 Iraqi occupation of Kuwait, pays some 20 million dinars a year in debt financing, a burden that Meshari suggests the state could shoulder with increased revenue from higher world oil prices.
Meshari said a recent decision by the state to inject 100 million dinars into KAC will help it service its debts of 230 million dinars but more measures were still needed.
KAC now has a fleet of 15 Airbus Industries aircraft all bought after the war and two Boeing Co 747s which will be replaced by two Boeing 777s on order.
KAC has no immediate fleet expansion plans. "For now, we will stop at a fleet of 17 aircraft" serving 42 destinations, he added.
KAC's assets were estimated at 723 million dinars at the end of 1996 -- a rise of 179 percent since 1991 when a U.S.-led military coalition forced Iraq out of Kuwait.
"Before the (1990 Iraqi) invasion KAC made profit, and it had liquidity and investments...KAC is probably one of the interests which suffered huge direct losses due to the invasion," said Meshari.
It lost 14 aircraft during the crisis and has sold off a remaining fleet of three Boeing 727s, two of four 747s and a 767.

In the first six months of 1996/97 KAC's passenger load factor was 69 percent, almost unchanged from the same period the previous year. Passenger revenue, 84 percent of total income, was 70.6 million dinars, while cargo, 14 percent of the total, earned the company 11.5 million dinars during the same period.
